final.memo:
When we purchased our stake in PetroChina in 2002–03, we did so because the market price represented a significant discount to our appraisal of the business's earning power and assets [D07]. We viewed this as a price-to-value gap rather than a permanent franchise holding of the type we might keep indefinitely [D07, S2].

Since that time, the company has seen its annual profitability rise materially, and the market has finally recognized this growth in the stock's valuation [D02, D07]. With the shares now trading at a P/E of approximately 14.5x, the market value has caught up with our estimate of intrinsic value [D04]. In such cases, the prudent course is to sell, as the margin of safety that originally justified the purchase no longer exists [S2].

While the company remains a large and capable oil and gas producer, we are not interested in holding the stock for its own sake once the investment thesis has been fulfilled [D01, S2]. We prefer to realize our gains—despite the tax consequences—and deploy that capital elsewhere, either into businesses with more attractive long-term prospects or into our own shares if the price is right [D06, D08].
